I farm in Quzhou County on the North China Plain, so at the start of the growing season I would stay with the system that fits my land, water conditions, and labor best: a winter wheat and summer maize rotation on most of my fields, with a smaller block of peanuts to spread risk and improve soil structure. I am 60, educated, and I would favor crops and management that are technically sound but not unnecessarily complicated. Wheat and maize are the most dependable cash-and-food combination for my area, the machinery and input markets around me support them well, and I know how to manage them tightly. I would use improved or hybrid seed rather than traditional seed because I care more about stable yield, disease resistance, and stand uniformity than seed saving. For fertilizer, I would keep nitrogen moderate instead of chasing maximum yield, because excess nitrogen raises lodging and disease risk and wastes money. I would apply phosphorus and potassium as a base to support root growth, grain filling, and resilience. For tillage, I would mostly use rotary tillage because it matches common local practice and lets me prepare land quickly between crops, while keeping operations manageable. For irrigation, I would give wheat more water than maize because wheat in my area is more exposed to spring moisture stress, while maize usually benefits from summer rainfall but still needs supplemental water if the monsoon is uneven. I would keep pesticide use limited and timed to actual field pressure rather than spraying heavily by habit. On the peanut block, I would use somewhat lighter nitrogen and better potassium balance, because peanuts fix part of their own nitrogen and respond well to balanced nutrition. Overall, I would choose a practical, risk-controlled plan: stable cereals on most land, one cash/oil crop on a smaller area, moderate inputs, careful water use, and yields that are realistic for Quzhou rather than overly optimistic.
